task.goal: Design a three-minute shadow performance for a senior center using everyday objects and no projector.
hard_constraints: One lamp and a white sheet are available; avoid darkening exits or creating trip hazards.
Audience members may have limited vision or hearing, so the story cannot rely on silhouettes alone.
Two performers have 20 minutes to set up and must leave the room as found.
task.available_resources: Lamp, sheet, chairs, ordinary objects and two performers.
task.expected_result: An expressive, repeatable performance with an inclusive audience check.

DIRECT_FULL.title: The Spoon That Found a Place
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: a narrated object story turns an ordinary spoon from an outsider into a useful member of a kitchen orchestra. Recognition, rejection and welcome provide the emotional arc; synchronized speech, shadows and gentle object sounds carry the same events through different senses.

Score: 0:00–0:25, one performer shows the actual spoon beside the sheet and says, “This spoon wanted somewhere to belong.” 0:25–1:10, behind the sheet, the spoon approaches a cup and a bowl; the narrator names each encounter and voices their initially dismissive replies. 1:10–2:10, the spoon discovers it can gently tap both objects into a shared rhythm. 2:10–2:40, the three silhouettes gather while the narrator says, “Different sounds, one table.” 2:40–3:00, show the actual objects again and ask, “Did the spoon find a place?” Accept speech, a nod or a raised hand without requiring participation.

Needs: a spoon, an unbreakable cup and bowl, and a lamp that produces readable shadows. One performer narrates in view; the other handles objects. Use a small sheet panel secured to stable chair backs outside circulation routes, with the lamp behind it. Keep exits and normal room lighting visible; route its cord entirely within the performance area. Allow 12 minutes to set up, five to rehearse and three to inspect safety. Restore chairs, sheet and objects afterward.

Limits: ambient light may weaken contrast, and object sounds may be inaudible. Spoken description and the visible object introduction are essential. The ending invites belonging without asking residents to disclose personal experiences.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: From the farthest intended seat, compare a 20-second narrated encounter with the same encounter played silently. Ask a willing viewer what approached what and what changed. Before starting, check whether the spoon is visible and the ordinary speaking voice is audible; move the performance closer or increase object separation if needed. If the narrated version still leaves the action unclear, simplify to two objects. Treat the final audience question as an invitation, not a memory test; silence does not establish failure or success.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A Rainstorm We Make Together
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: synchronized sound and shadow create a shared sensory event rather than a character plot. Optional audience participation changes the intensity of an imagined rainstorm, making the room’s collective action the dramatic engine.

Score: 0:00–0:30, the visible performer introduces a crumpled-paper cloud and says, “We will make a little rain, then let it pass. Watching is enough.” Offer an optional seated finger-rubbing gesture; demonstrate it clearly. 0:30–1:15, the second performer slowly moves the cloud across the sheet while the leader describes the gathering weather and softly rustles paper. 1:15–2:00, spread fingers cast falling-rain shadows; the leader invites gentle fingertip taps on participants’ own palms. No thunder, sudden volume changes or standing. 2:00–2:35, the leader visibly slows both hands, says, “The rain is easing,” and reduces the rustling as the cloud leaves. 2:35–3:00, a large cardboard sun appears, accompanied by “The sun is back.” Ask, “Keep the sunshine, or have one last little raindrop?” Accept a spoken choice or a demonstrated gesture, then give a brief corresponding ending.

Needs: paper, a large cardboard circle, lamp, sheet and stable chairs. One performer leads in view and provides all verbal weather cues; the other makes shadows. Set up a secured sheet panel and contained lamp cord away from exits in 10 minutes, rehearse cues for seven and inspect sightlines for three. Leave room lighting on and restore the room afterward.

Limits: participation must remain optional, and subtle sounds will not reach everyone. Large movements and spoken cues supply parallel information. The piece works with no audience response, although its participatory effect remains uncertain until tried.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Prototype 30 seconds of increasing and decreasing rain. Compare the coordinated version with paper rustling alone. Ask a willing viewer whether the weather was growing or easing, and whether the invitation felt easy to decline. Check from a distant seat that the leader’s hands and cloud are distinguishable. If cues compete or produce confusion, remove audience tapping and retain one clearly demonstrated gesture. During the final choice, acknowledge any clear response without claiming it represents the whole room.

DIRECT_FULL.title: The Shadow Was Bigger Than the Problem
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: changing an object’s distance from the lamp changes its apparent size. An initially enormous shadow becomes a small, familiar object, turning a simple optical effect into a gentle story about looking again.

Score: 0:00–0:25, the visible narrator says, “Sometimes a small thing casts a very big shadow.” 0:25–1:05, the operator holds a clothespin close enough to the lamp to cast a large shape, without touching the lamp or blocking ventilation. The narrator describes what everyone is being shown: “A huge shape, with a mouth like a crocodile.” 1:05–1:45, move the clothespin toward the sheet so the shadow shrinks while saying, “Closer to the curtain, smaller and smaller.” 1:45–2:10, bring the actual clothespin into view: “Only a clothespin! Useful for keeping two things together.” 2:10–2:40, repeat the transformation once with an open hand, explicitly naming it as it changes from a large tree shape into an ordinary hand. 2:40–3:00, offer the clothespin large and small again and ask, “Which shall take the final bow?” Accept a word, gesture or no response; finish with both sizes if nobody chooses.

Needs: a large clothespin, lamp, sheet and stable chairs. One performer narrates in view; the other controls distance. This requires a lamp with a sufficiently compact light source and enough contained space between lamp and sheet. Spend eight setup minutes testing the optical effect before committing, seven securing the panel and cord outside walking routes, and five rehearsing. Keep exits lit, avoid hot surfaces and restore the room afterward.

Limits: diffuse lamps can produce blurred shadows, and normal room lighting may reduce contrast. Narration explains every transformation, but the central visual surprise may remain inaccessible to some viewers. Keep the tone playful; do not imply that real worries are trivial.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Before setup proceeds, compare the clothespin held at two safe distances with the same object held still. From the farthest intended seat, ask a willing viewer whether the two sizes are visibly different and whether the spoken description explains the change. If neither size nor outline is clear under the existing room lighting, this alternative fails its central mechanism; select another performance rather than darkening circulation areas. Also check that the reveal reads as playful rather than frightening or patronizing.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A Bridge Made by Two
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: separate object shadows join to form a continuous bridge. Cooperation visibly changes what is possible: neither performer can complete the crossing alone. Spoken description and a visible demonstration carry the same causal story for people who cannot resolve the shadows.

Three-minute score: 0:00–0:30, show two books and a spoon in front of the sheet. Say, “Two banks, one traveler, and a gap.” Hold the books apart to demonstrate. 0:30–1:05, behind the sheet, one performer holds a book horizontally while the other moves the spoon toward its edge. The narrator says, “This side reaches halfway. The traveler waits.” 1:05–1:40, try the second book alone from the opposite side: “That side also reaches halfway.” Keep the mood curious, without falls or frightening sounds. 1:40–2:15, both performers align their book shadows into one broad path; one also carries the spoon slowly across. Describe the joining and crossing explicitly. 2:15–2:40, bring the actual objects forward and repeat the joining gesture where everyone can see the performers. 2:40–3:00, ask, “Show or tell us: did the crossing happen before the sides joined, or after?” Demonstrate both options; participation is optional. End by joining the books again.

Needs: two lightweight books, a spoon, two stable chairs, sheet and lamp. Both performers handle objects; one narrates throughout. The books remain handheld and support no weight. Use eight minutes to secure a small sheet panel to chair backs, five to test alignment, four to rehearse and three to inspect. Keep normal room and exit lighting on; contain the lamp, its cord and all objects outside walking routes, with fabric clear of the bulb. Record chair positions before moving them and restore everything afterward.

Assumptions and limits: the available lamp must produce a sufficiently clear joined outline. The crossing can remain understandable through narration, but indistinct shadows would weaken the cooperative reveal.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Run a 25-second crossing from the farthest intended seat. Compare two visibly separated book shadows with the joined version, using the same narration volume. Ask a willing viewer what allowed the traveler to cross and whether they could see the joining or follow its description. If the versions look identical, adjust object spacing once; if that fails, this staging does not support the mechanism. Separately check that both spoken options and demonstrated gestures are accessible. An unanswered final invitation is not evidence of misunderstanding.

DIRECT_FULL.title: The Table Remembers
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: repeat the same short table-setting ritual three times, changing its ending. Recognition of the repeated actions makes a small final change expressive: a solitary routine becomes an invitation. This uses rhythm, anticipation and human gesture rather than object characters or an optical surprise.

Three-minute score: 0:00–0:25, the visible narrator shows an unbreakable cup, a folded cloth and a second cup: “Every afternoon, someone prepares a place.” 0:25–0:55, behind the sheet, the second performer slowly unfolds the cloth, places one cup within the shadow area, then rests an open hand beside it. The narrator names each action: “Cloth. Cup. A moment to pause.” 0:55–1:25, repeat exactly, with the same words and timing. Introduce no loud sound cues. 1:25–2:00, begin the ritual a third time; after the first cup, add the second. Say, “Today, there is another place.” 2:00–2:30, the narrator joins the operator behind the sheet. Two open-hand shadows approach the cups and pause together. Continue speaking: “Two people share the afternoon.” 2:30–2:45, both return to view holding the actual cups and repeat the welcoming open-hand gesture. 2:45–3:00, ask, “Was the added place clear? You can tell us, nod, or show two fingers.” Thank the audience without requiring an answer.

Needs: two unbreakable cups, a cloth, sheet, lamp and stable chairs. A chair seat behind the sheet holds the objects; test whether its shadow leaves the hands and cups distinguishable. Spend eight setup minutes securing the panel and containing the cord, five testing the composition, four rehearsing the repeated timing and three inspecting routes and sightlines. Preserve room lighting and lit exits, keep fabric away from the bulb, and return chairs and objects to their original positions afterward.

Assumptions and limits: repetition must be slow enough to recognize without becoming tedious. The scene may evoke loneliness or bereavement; frame the extra place as an everyday welcome and avoid asking for personal memories. Narration conveys every change, while visible demonstrations support people who miss speech.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Prototype the repeated phrase and final addition in 40 seconds. Compare it with a single uninterrupted setting of two cups. Ask a willing viewer which version made the extra place feel meaningful, and whether either felt slow, sentimental or unclear. If repetition adds no anticipation, shorten each cycle while retaining the three-minute performance through longer welcoming gestures. Check speech audibility and the actual-object demonstration from a distant seat. If neither channel communicates the added place, reposition closer before performing; do not infer accessibility from polite applause.

DIRECT_FULL.title: The Shadow Learns to Wave
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: a visible performer and a separately operated shadow establish a copying game; the shadow then initiates a gesture that the person copies. Reversing who leads creates the story: a follower becomes a partner. Clear spoken descriptions, visible actions and large shadow movements communicate the same change.

Three-minute score: 0:00–0:30, introduce a mitten or oven glove: “My friend behind this curtain likes to copy me.” Show the actual glove and demonstrate an open-handed greeting. 0:30–1:10, the visible performer makes three slow movements beside the sheet: hand up, hand sideways, hand down. The operator copies each with the glove shadow while the visible performer names the action. 1:10–1:40, the person raises a hand, but the shadow stays down. Pause: “I moved. My friend is waiting. Perhaps it wants a turn.” Avoid framing this as a mistake. 1:40–2:15, the shadow waves first. The person says, “You waved first! Now I’ll follow,” then visibly copies it. Repeat with one slow sideways movement. 2:15–2:40, both wave together: “We can take turns leading.” 2:40–3:00, ask, “Could you follow the change of leader? A word, nod or gesture is welcome; watching is enough.” Finish with a shared bow.

Needs: one glove, lamp, sheet and stable chairs. Assume the sheet can be securely attached using available clips or ties; do not balance loose fabric precariously. One performer remains visible and speaks; the other operates the glove. Allocate eight setup minutes to the screen and contained cord, five to sightlines, four to cue rehearsal and three to safety inspection. Preserve room and exit lighting, keep fabric clear of the lamp, and place everything outside walking routes. Note original chair positions and restore the room afterward.

Limits: this depends on viewers distinguishing person and shadow. Description supports limited vision; large visible gestures support limited hearing. Neither guarantees access for someone who cannot use either channel.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Rehearse a 30-second copy-and-reversal sequence, then a version where the person always leads. From a distant intended seat, ask a willing viewer whether the relationship changed and which version made that clearer. Also ask whether speech and gestures were accessible, without treating silence as agreement. If the reversal is unclear, increase the pause and repeat “You first; I’ll follow” once. If person and shadow remain indistinguishable under normal lighting, this staging fails its central mechanism; do not compensate by darkening exits. Time one complete run to verify the three-minute score.

EXPAND.title: The Shadow That Was Always Late
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: a visible performer and a separately operated shadow repeat the same simple actions at different times. Predictable delay creates gentle comedy; their eventual synchronization supplies the ending. Unlike the spoon story, the expressive action comes from timing and imitation rather than object rejection and welcome.

Score: 0:00–0:30, the visible performer raises an open hand and introduces its partner: “My shadow likes to take its time.” The operator casts a hand shadow onto the sheet. 0:30–1:15, the visible performer waves, rests, then raises a spoon; the shadow copies each action two seconds later. The visible performer describes both events: “I waved. Now my shadow waves.” 1:15–2:00, reverse the lead: “Perhaps I should follow.” The shadow slowly waves and raises its spoon; the visible performer follows late. 2:00–2:35, both settle into three slow, simultaneous waves, verbally marked “Together.” 2:35–3:00, both bow. Ask, “Was that pace comfortable?” Accept a word, gesture or no response.

Preparation: use two spoons, lamp, sheet and stable chairs. Spend eight minutes positioning a small sheet panel securely over chair backs, five checking light and cord containment, and seven rehearsing the fixed pauses. Keep the visible performer beside the sheet, facing the audience. All equipment stays outside circulation routes; retain room and exit lighting, keep fabric clear of lamp heat, and avoid unsecured or improvised elevated supports. Record chair positions before moving them and restore everything afterward.

Prerequisites and limits: the operator must see the partner or hear clear cues. Large, separated movements and spoken descriptions carry the sequence, but some viewers may miss the visual joke. If safe, readable shadows cannot be obtained, this staging is unsuitable.
EXPAND.experiment: The visible performer owns a one-minute rehearsal with a willing viewer at the farthest intended seat. Compare the delayed sequence with a synchronized version using the same actions and words. Ask which felt clearer and whether either was amusing or confusing; also check voice audibility and shadow visibility. Stop developing the delay if it adds confusion without expressive benefit, or if maintaining it forces rushed speech. Before the full performance, offer seated viewers an optional visibility-and-audibility check; bring the performance area closer only if circulation remains clear. Silence is not evidence of comprehension.

EXPAND.title: A Door Made of Empty Space
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: two ordinary objects form a meaningful opening through the light left between their shadows. Attention shifts from recognizing individual silhouettes to discovering negative space. This creates a visual act of construction, distinct from the prior size-change illusion or the spoon’s narrated social encounters.

Score: 0:00–0:30, show two closed books in ordinary room light: “Two books can make a little doorway. Watch the light between them.” 0:30–1:10, the operator places the books upright near the sheet, casting two broad, separated shadows. The narrator describes the bright passage between them and holds both hands apart visibly. 1:10–1:50, move one book slowly inward until the passage closes: “The doorway has closed.” The narrator brings their hands together. 1:50–2:25, reopen the gap generously: “Now there is room to come through.” A spoon travels through the bright opening, accompanied by an explicit description of its passage. 2:25–2:45, leave the doorway open and repeat the passage once. 2:45–3:00, show the actual books again: “We made a doorway out of light.” Invite an optional open-hands gesture as the final bow.

Preparation: one performer narrates and demonstrates the opening in view; the other operates books and spoon. Use a secured sheet panel over stable chair backs, with books supported on a stable chair seat behind it. Allocate ten minutes to assembly and optical testing, seven to rehearsal and three to safety inspection. Contain the lamp cord inside the performance footprint, keep fabric away from heat, preserve lit exits and walking routes, and restore the original chair arrangement afterward.

Prerequisites and limits: the available geometry must yield a bright gap large enough to distinguish from the farthest seat. The visible hand demonstration and narration repeat its meaning, but the visual discovery remains uncertain for viewers with limited vision. Never ask residents to approach or pass through equipment.
EXPAND.experiment: The narrator owns a 30-second comparison: first present a doorway outlined by hands, then construct the doorway between book shadows with the same spoken description. Ask a willing viewer what opened and whether the shadow version added anything expressive. Check both the farthest sightline and whether book handling is stable. Stop this route if the gap cannot be read without reducing circulation lighting, if books require precarious support, or if assembly adds effort without improving the experience over the simple hand version. At entry, invite a voluntary word or gesture indicating whether the bright opening and narrator are accessible.

EXPAND.title: The Audience Sees the Trick
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: show an ordinary object and its theatrical transformation at the same time. A visible operator makes a tea towel’s shadow become a bird, openly demonstrating how motion creates an imagined character. The pleasure comes from knowingly holding the real object and imagined creature together; neither concealment nor identifying an unexplained silhouette is necessary.

Score: 0:00–0:30, the narrator displays a tea towel: “A towel. With a little movement, we can imagine a bird.” 0:30–1:10, the operator stands beside the sheet, in audience view, and folds the towel over one hand within the lamp beam. Slowly lift and lower its corners. The narrator says, “The towel lifts; our bird spreads its wings.” 1:10–1:50, let the towel settle: “The wings rest.” Repeat the transition from towel to bird twice, leaving a clear pause between states. 1:50–2:25, the narrator holds out an open palm beside the shadow: “Here is a place to land.” The operator lowers the shadow toward it without physical contact. 2:25–2:40, unfold and show the towel: “And here is our towel again.” 2:40–3:00, ask, “Would you like one more slow wingbeat?” Accept speech or gesture; if there is no response, give one gentle wingbeat and finish.

Preparation: two performers, tea towel, lamp, sheet and stable chairs suffice. Spend eight minutes finding a side angle that shows both towel and shadow, seven securing the panel and containing the cord, and five rehearsing. Keep performers stationary within a clear footprint, exits and room lighting on, and towel and sheet safely clear of lamp heat. Note the room arrangement and restore it afterward.

Prerequisites and limits: a workable side sightline is essential. Compared with the prior clothespin reveal, this removes the need to withhold the object’s identity or make a large size transformation. It may sacrifice surprise, and visible manipulation can divide attention. Spoken descriptions and the plainly visible towel carry every change.
EXPAND.experiment: The narrator owns a 45-second prototype comparing exposed manipulation with the same towel motion performed behind the sheet, using identical narration. Ask a willing viewer which version was easier to follow and whether seeing the towel helped or distracted. Inspect from the farthest intended seat and an off-center seat. Stop the exposed version if its required angle narrows audience access, blocks circulation, or provides no clarity or expressive gain over concealed operation. Begin the actual performance with an optional check that viewers can see either the towel or shadow and hear the narration; adjust position or pace before continuing.

EXPAND.title: The Spoon Finds Its Beat — With a Restart Cue
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: “The Spoon That Found a Place.” Preserve its narrated belonging story, visible object introduction, gentle rhythm and optional closing question. Change: add an explicit recovery action for lost timing or interruption. The narrator owns the pause; the operator stops tapping and holds the objects still. The narrator says, “Here is our spoon, finding its place at the table,” names the objects again, then counts three slow beats before both resume. Resume at the welcoming rhythm, skipping remaining rejection dialogue. This gives the performers a shared restart without extending the performance.

Three-minute score: 0:00–0:25, show spoon, unbreakable cup and bowl and introduce the spoon’s wish to belong. 0:25–1:05, narrate its unsuccessful approaches, explicitly naming each action. 1:05–2:10, discover a gentle shared tapping rhythm. 2:10–2:40, gather their shadows: “Different sounds, one table.” 2:40–3:00, show the objects and invite, “Did the spoon find a place?” Accept speech, nod, gesture or no response. After a substantial interruption, use the restart and go directly to the final gathering and question.

Needs: two performers, spoon, unbreakable cup and bowl, lamp, sheet and stable chairs. One narrates in view; one operates. Use 10 minutes to establish a securely supported sheet and contained cord, five to rehearse including recovery, and five to check access and safety. Keep normal room and exit lighting, walking routes clear, and fabric away from lamp heat. If available chairs cannot safely support the sheet, do not improvise an unstable rig. Note original positions and restore everything afterward.

Compared with the source, the restart costs one short rehearsal but may prevent an interruption becoming a confusing sequence. This benefit is untested. Narration, visible objects and sounds provide parallel information, but cannot guarantee access for someone with substantial combined vision and hearing loss. Before starting, invite an optional visibility-and-audibility response; adjust spacing, position or delivery within the safe footprint. If access remains inadequate, offer the spoken and visible object story while acknowledging that the shadow component is inaccessible.
EXPAND.experiment: The narrator owns a one-minute prototype from the farthest intended seat with a willing viewer. Show one encounter and the welcoming rhythm; deliberately interrupt once, then use the restart. Ask what the spoon wanted, what changed, and whether restarting helped or repeated too much. Check shadow visibility and voice audibility separately. Stop the tapping if it masks speech; retain spoken beat counts. If the restart still obscures the story, simplify to spoon and cup and rehearse once more. If the sheet support or cord arrangement is unsafe, stop that staging. The final audience invitation is optional; silence establishes neither comprehension nor failure.

EXPAND.title: Rain That Can Become Quiet
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: “A Rainstorm We Make Together.” Preserve its gathering cloud, gentle rain, easing weather, optional seated participation and sunshine ending. Change: give the visible leader a practiced way to reduce stimulation immediately, including when someone cannot comfortably make the proposed gesture. Before beginning, say and demonstrate, “You may watch, join in, or ask for quiet with a word or raised palm.” The leader watches the audience and owns the response. Any clear request for quiet, or apparent discomfort, triggers “The rain is easing now”; the operator stops rustling, both lower their hands, and the leader advances to sunshine. Participation is never needed to continue.

Three-minute score: 0:00–0:30, show a paper cloud, explain the quiet signal and invite optional finger rubbing. 0:30–1:15, move the cloud slowly across the sheet while naming the gathering weather. 1:15–2:00, cast large finger-rain shadows and invite gentle taps on participants’ own palms. 2:00–2:35, visibly slow hands and describe the easing rain. 2:35–3:00, show a large paper sun and ask, “Was that pace and sound comfortable?” Accept words, gestures or no answer. If quiet is requested earlier, hold a calm sunshine tableau through the remaining sequence rather than restarting rain.

Needs: paper, lamp, sheet, stable chairs and two performers. One leads visibly and describes every transition; the other operates shadows and paper sounds. Allocate 10 setup minutes, seven rehearsal minutes including the quiet transition, and three for sightlines, audibility and safety. Secure the sheet only where existing supports are stable; contain the cord, preserve lit exits and walking routes, and separate fabric from lamp heat. Restore the original arrangement afterward.

Compared with the source, this adds a clear action after a comfort concern instead of relying on optional participation alone. It costs introductory time and may shorten the storm, but retains its expressive rise and release. Its effectiveness is uncertain: a signal may be missed, and some people cannot use it. The leader therefore also responds to visible discomfort without requiring an explanation. Spoken cues and large visible gestures supplement shadows and soft sounds.
EXPAND.experiment: The visible leader owns a 40-second prototype with a willing viewer at a distant seat. Check whether the cloud, leader’s hands and spoken weather changes are accessible. Have the viewer try either a spoken quiet request or raised palm during the rain; the operator must stop sound on the leader’s easing cue. Ask whether the invitation felt optional and whether the quiet transition was clear. Stop the sound layer if it competes with speech or causes discomfort; continue with described weather and slow gestures. If the leader cannot monitor viewers while performing, remove audience tapping and reduce the sequence to cloud, easing and sunshine. Do not treat an unanswered comfort question as approval.

EXPAND.title: One Cup, Three Times of Day
EXPAND.proposal:
New mechanism: repetition changes the meaning of an unchanged image. The same cup shadow and lifting gesture return at morning, afternoon and evening; narration and vocal rhythm make the repetitions feel hopeful, companionable and restful. This removes the assumption that a shadow performance needs recognizable moving characters, optical transformations or precise synchronization. The cup remains an ordinary cup throughout.

Three-minute score: 0:00–0:25, the visible narrator shows an empty, unbreakable cup: “One cup. Three small pauses in a day.” Briefly check whether the audience can hear the voice and see the cup or shadow. 0:25–1:05, the operator slowly lifts and lowers the cup behind the sheet while the narrator says, brightly but without shouting, “Morning. A warm drink. The day can begin.” Repeat the lift once. 1:05–1:45, repeat exactly the same movement: “Afternoon. A pause for company. You are welcome here.” The narrator gives a visible welcoming gesture. 1:45–2:25, repeat more slowly: “Evening. The work is done. Time to rest.” 2:25–2:40, show the actual cup again: “The same cup, holding three different moments.” 2:40–3:00, invite, “Which moment shall take our bow: morning, afternoon or evening?” Accept a word or gesture; if no clear choice emerges, say all three and bow. Reserve the final five seconds for this default ending.

Needs: one cup, lamp, sheet, stable chairs and two performers. The narrator owns timing and audience contact; the operator only lifts, lowers and holds. Prepare the safe sheet and lamp arrangement in 10 minutes, rehearse for seven, and inspect access and safety for three. Keep exits and ordinary room lighting on, cords within the performance footprint, and cloth clear of lamp heat. Record chair positions and restore the room afterward. No liquid or audience object handling is needed.

Compared with the spoon story, this requires fewer props and handling cues, but sacrifices a stronger plot and may feel repetitive. Its expressive value depends on delivery and audience response; it is not established. Explicit time-of-day narration carries the sequence when silhouettes are unclear. If the lamp produces only a blurred patch, switch to the visible cup version; this preserves the story but does not fully achieve the intended shadow performance. If safe sheet support is unavailable, do not erect it.
EXPAND.experiment: The narrator owns a 45-second prototype: perform the same cup lift twice, first as morning and then as evening, using the proposed words and pacing. Ask a willing viewer at the farthest intended seat whether the moments felt different and whether the repetition was pleasant or slow. Also check voice audibility and the visibility of both cup and shadow. Stop developing this route if the changed context adds no expressive meaning after one rehearsal; a simple narrated object story is then the stronger choice. During the full performance, respond to an access concern by pausing, adjusting delivery or position safely, and repeating the current time-of-day sentence once. If that fails, use the visible cup fallback and acknowledge the shadow limitation.
